description: Delta-177 is a Dushanbe-based team. I’m a backend developer (C#/.NET, ASP.NET, SQL) learning Python and machine learning. We plan to tackle “Field Shift”: a tool that uses NASA satellite data to help farmers in Tajikistan choose climate-resilient crop rotations. Looking for: Python/data enthusiasts, someone with agriculture or ecology knowledge, a UI/UX designer, and a confident presenter. Team language: Tajik/Russian, English welcome!
summary:
Field Shift Tajikistan is a free, farmer-friendly web tool that turns NASA Earth data into crop-rotation advice for farmers in Tajikistan. A farmer picks a field on a satellite map and tells us the current rotation, the previous crop, available irrigation water and what matters most: saving water, income, soil health or livestock feed. The tool then loads 24 years of daily NASA POWER data for that exact point (temperature, rainfall, root-zone soil wetness, solar radiation) and 2 years of NASA MODIS NDVI greenness, and compares the current rotation with three alternatives: a summer mung bean and winter cover crop after wheat, an alfalfa-based soil-restoring rotation, and a drought-tolerant option.

For each strategy it shows water needs by month, bare-field periods, heat and frost risks, and long-term climate trends. It also explains why the option was suggested, the evidence, the benefits, the risks to check locally and the information gaps. “What if” sliders test drier or hotter futures. The interface works in Tajik, Russian and English and runs in any browser, including on phones.

Central Asian farmers face rising heat, water shortages and depleted soils. Field Shift supports, rather than replaces, their judgment with open NASA data.

Field Shift was built by Team Delta-177, two brothers from Dushanbe who want to help farmers in Tajikistan. 
Local soil data is not yet included (SoilGrids is planned).

details:
What it does and how it works
Field Shift is a decision-support web app that helps farmers in Tajikistan choose crop rotations that save water, protect soil and cope with a changing climate. The farmer answers four simple questions: where the field is (satellite map, village search or “my location”), what is grown now and what grew before, how much irrigation water is available, and what matters most (water, income, soil health or livestock feed). The app then:

  1. Downloads 24 years (2001–2024) of daily NASA POWER data for that exact point: air temperature (min/max/mean), corrected precipitation, root-zone soil wetness and solar radiation.
  2. Computes reference evapotranspiration (FAO-56 Hargreaves), monthly crop water needs (ETo × crop coefficient minus effective rain), heat days above 35 °C, frost dates, heat units available after the wheat harvest, and climate trends per decade.
  3. Loads 2 years of NASA MODIS NDVI (MOD13Q1, 250 m) to show when the field was actually green or bare, and offers NASA GIBS layers (MODIS true colour, NDVI, land surface temperature) on the map.
  4. Compares the current rotation with three alternatives (wheat + summer mung bean + winter vetch; alfalfa 3 years → cotton → wheat; wheat → forage sorghum → chickpea), scores them by the farmer’s own priorities and penalises options that need more water than the farm has.
  5. Gives one clear answer (“Our advice”) and, for every strategy, explains why it was suggested, the evidence, the benefits, the risks to check locally and the information gaps.

Benefits and intended impact
Farmers get a transparent, data-based way to fill bare summer months, add nitrogen-fixing crops, reduce irrigation and prepare for hotter, drier years. “What if” sliders (rainfall −50% to +30%, temperature +0 to +3 °C) let them test future scenarios. Results can be shared by link or printed for a family member or an agronomist. Our aim is to bring open NASA data to smallholders who have never used satellite data, starting in Khatlon and Sughd.

Tools and technologies
HTML, CSS and JavaScript (a single page that works in any browser, including phones, with no installation); Leaflet maps with Esri World Imagery and OpenStreetMap; Plotly.js charts; the NASA POWER daily point API; the NASA GIBS WMTS imagery service; the ORNL DAAC MODIS web service; OpenStreetMap Nominatim for village search. An earlier prototype was built in Python (Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, Plotly, Folium). We used an AI coding assistant (Claude) to speed up development. No special hardware is required.

What makes it creative

  • It turns raw climate data into one question a farmer really asks: “What should I plant next, and why?”
  • It combines long-term climate (NASA POWER) with what the field actually looked like (MODIS NDVI) to confirm bare-field periods.
  • It takes the previous crop into account (same plant family = disease risk, legumes = nitrogen bonus).
  • It shows the ~50 km NASA POWER data cell on the map so users see the data’s real resolution.
  • It works in Tajik, Russian and English.

Factors we considered

  • Low technical and geospatial experience of users: plain words, big buttons, a glossary of terms like ETo and NDVI.
  • Weak hardware and internet: no installation, data cached in the browser.
  • Water scarcity as the main local constraint.
  • Local crops and practices (cotton–wheat systems, alfalfa, mung bean).
  • Honesty about uncertainty: coarse data resolution, no field soil test, expert-estimated crop indices.
  • No promises of yields or profit: the tool supports, not replaces, farmer and agronomist judgment.
